h1: FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor for Buyers, Agents and Lenders
lede: Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor. We are proud of that designation because it lets us help increase home ownership and revitalize neighborhoods at the same time. An FHA 203(k) loan lets an eligible buyer or homeowner finance qualifying repairs as part of a purchase or refinance mortgage. We handle the renovation side: the scope, the bid, the documentation the lender needs and the work itself.

sections.body:
An FHA 203(k) loan allows eligible homebuyers and homeowners to finance qualifying repairs and renovations as part of a purchase or refinance mortgage. Instead of buying a house with one loan and paying for repairs with cash, credit cards or a second loan, the buyer rolls eligible renovation costs into a single FHA-insured mortgage.

That changes which houses are realistic for many buyers. A move-in-ready house and a dated house that needs a new kitchen, a roof and an electrical update can both be within reach, because the repair money is part of the financing rather than an out-of-pocket hurdle after closing. For neighborhoods with older housing stock, it also means houses that might have sat vacant or gone to investors can go to owner-occupants who will fix them up and stay.

The program has rules that shape how the renovation is planned and paid for. The renovation funds are not handed to the buyer at closing. They are held and released as the work is completed, based on the approved scope and the lender's process. The scope and the contractor's bid are reviewed by the lender, and depending on which version of the program is used, a 203(k) Consultant may be involved from the start.

Because of those rules, the contractor matters more on a 203(k) than on a typical renovation. The contractor has to produce a bid detailed enough for the lender and consultant to approve, perform work that matches the approved scope, document progress for draw releases and stay within the program's eligibility rules. That is the work an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor is set up to do.

There are two types of 203(k) loans, and choosing the right one depends mostly on the size and nature of the work.

The Standard 203(k) is designed for major rehabilitation, structural work and more complex renovation projects. Eligible improvements can include structural alterations, major remodeling, additions, foundation work and certain conversions of one- to four-unit properties. Standard 203(k) may also be used when rehabilitation costs exceed the $75,000 limit for the Limited 203(k), subject to applicable FHA mortgage limits and other program requirements. On a Standard 203(k), rehabilitation costs must total at least $5,000, and an FHA-approved 203(k) Consultant is required.

The Limited 203(k) is for minor remodeling and nonstructural repairs with total rehabilitation costs up to $75,000. For projects over $15,000, an inspection is required. For projects of $15,000 or less, the lender may determine whether an inspection is necessary. A 203(k) Consultant is optional for the Limited 203(k), although a lender may require one.

In short:

- Standard: structural work, additions, foundation repair, major remodels, certain one-to-four unit conversions, or any eligible project above the Limited cap. Minimum of $5,000 in rehabilitation costs. Consultant required.
- Limited: nonstructural repairs and minor remodeling up to $75,000 in total rehabilitation costs. Inspection required above $15,000, at the lender's discretion at or below it. Consultant optional unless the lender requires one.

If you are unsure which version fits, start with the scope. Once we know what the house actually needs, the right program is usually clear, and your lender makes the final call.

The two versions of the program suit different kinds of houses, and it helps buyers and agents to recognize the difference early in the search.

A Limited 203(k) tends to fit a house that is structurally sound but dated or worn. Typical examples are a home that needs a kitchen update, a bathroom remodel, new flooring and paint, a replacement furnace or water heater, a roof, new windows, or an electrical or plumbing update. None of that requires moving walls or touching the foundation, and the work can be scoped and priced cleanly.

A Standard 203(k) tends to fit a house with bigger problems or bigger plans. Examples include foundation settlement or a failing basement wall, a sagging floor system or roof structure, an addition to create another bedroom or bath, a layout change that removes a bearing wall, or the conversion of a property within the one-to-four unit range. A house with a long list of issues that pushes the rehabilitation total beyond the Limited cap also belongs in the Standard program.

Older houses deserve particular care during scoping. Homes built before 1978 may contain lead-based paint, and houses from the middle decades of the last century can contain asbestos in flooring, pipe insulation or siding. Knob-and-tube wiring, galvanized supply lines and old cast-iron drains are common in older stock. These conditions affect cost and sometimes which program fits, so we look for them before the bid is written rather than after the loan closes.

Our estimators can walk a property with the buyer or agent and help sort out whether the likely scope points toward Limited or Standard.

sections.h2: For homebuyers: one mortgage, more choices
sections.body:
For homebuyers, the main benefit is the ability to finance eligible purchase and renovation costs through a single mortgage. That expands the range of homes you can consider to include properties that need repairs or updates, which in many markets are the houses priced within reach. Depending on the project, renovations may be completed before or after you move in.

The process feels different from a regular purchase, and knowing what to expect helps. Talk with an FHA-approved lender first to confirm your eligibility and learn how they handle 203(k) loans, because lenders differ in how they run the program. Once you have a house in mind, the contractor walks the property and prepares a detailed scope and bid. On a Standard 203(k), the consultant also inspects the house and prepares a write-up of the required and requested work. The lender reviews the bid and paperwork before closing.

One restriction surprises some buyers: most lenders do not allow buyers to perform the renovations themselves. The work has to be done by a contractor, which protects the buyer, the lender and the value of the house.

When Genstone is your contractor, you get a detailed scope document and estimate showing anticipated labor and materials, and a designated field manager who serves as your primary point of contact through the work. Our team coordinates required permits and inspections. You can follow progress and documentation without being on site, which matters if you are still living elsewhere while the work is done. Completed work carries a one-year workmanship warranty.

sections.h2: For real estate agents: a wider set of houses to show
sections.body:
For agents, the 203(k) program means you can help buyers consider properties that need repairs instead of limiting the search to move-in-ready inventory. In tight markets, that can be the difference between a buyer who keeps losing bidding wars on finished houses and a buyer who closes on a home with room to improve.

A few habits help 203(k) deals go smoothly:

- Bring a contractor in early. The lender needs a detailed bid before closing, and the bid depends on a proper walk-through. The sooner the contractor sees the house, the less pressure there is on the contract timeline.
- Set expectations about the timeline. A 203(k) purchase involves more steps than a standard FHA purchase, including the bid review and, on a Standard 203(k), the consultant's inspection and write-up. Build realistic contingency periods into the offer.
- Match the house to the program. A buyer who falls for a house that needs structural work should know it will likely be a Standard 203(k) with a required consultant.
- Keep luxury items out of the plan. New pools, spas and outdoor kitchens are not eligible, and a buyer counting on them will be disappointed.

Genstone can walk a property with you and your buyer, give an early read on the likely scope, and produce the detailed bid the lender needs. Because we coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors under a designated field manager, the buyer gets one accountable point of contact from bid through completion, and you get a contractor who understands how 203(k) transactions run.

sections.h2: For lenders: a contractor built for 203(k) documentation
sections.body:
For lenders, the value of a 203(k) contractor is measured in paperwork as much as workmanship. You need an experienced renovation contractor capable of developing detailed scopes and estimates and completing work through the 203(k) process without creating problems for your underwriters, your consultants or your draw desk.

Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor, and our process is built around documentation. Our bids are itemized by labor and materials so they can be reconciled against the consultant's write-up on a Standard 203(k) or reviewed directly on a Limited 203(k). The scope is specific about quantities, locations and materials, which reduces back-and-forth during approval.

During construction, a designated field manager oversees the work and keeps progress documented with photos and milestones. Draw requests line up with completed work, which makes them straightforward for the consultant or inspector to verify. Lien waivers are collected as part of our risk-management process, and we verify that the contractors assigned to the project maintain appropriate insurance and applicable licensing requirements. Permits and inspections are coordinated by our team.

When unforeseen conditions arise, such as hidden rot or a failed drain line uncovered during demolition, we document the condition and the cost impact and work through the change process with the borrower and the lender before additional work proceeds.

Genstone also works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs and Government-Sponsored Enterprises on renovation and REO work, so we are accustomed to institutional documentation standards and reporting expectations.

sections.h2: Important restrictions to keep in mind
sections.body:
The 203(k) program covers a wide range of work, but a few restrictions come up often enough that every buyer, agent and lender should know them.

- Eligible renovations: most repairs and renovations are permitted, including pool repairs. Luxury additions such as new pools, spas and outdoor kitchens are not eligible.
- Who completes the work: most lenders do not allow buyers to perform the renovations themselves.
- Multifamily properties: FHA 203(k) loans may be used for eligible two- to four-unit properties, provided the buyer occupies one of the units.

The two-to-four unit option is worth a closer look. A buyer can purchase a duplex, triplex or fourplex, renovate the building through the 203(k) and live in one unit while renting the others. Renovating occupied or partially occupied small multifamily buildings takes careful phasing, and shared systems such as roofs, boilers, water service and electrical services often need attention across the whole building. Genstone renovates small multifamily properties for investors as well as owner-occupants, so we are familiar with those challenges.

The program's other rules, including FHA mortgage limits and lender-specific requirements, come from HUD and the lender rather than the contractor. We plan the scope around them but do not make eligibility decisions. That is why the right first step is always a conversation with an FHA-approved lender to determine eligibility.

Once the lender is in place, contact Genstone Construction at (312) 429-2637 to discuss your renovation scope and project.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a Standard and a Limited 203(k)?
faqs.a: The Standard 203(k) is for major rehabilitation, structural work, additions, foundation work, certain one-to-four unit conversions, and projects above the $75,000 Limited cap. It requires at least $5,000 in rehabilitation costs and an FHA-approved 203(k) Consultant. The Limited 203(k) covers minor remodeling and nonstructural repairs up to $75,000. A consultant is optional unless the lender requires one, and an inspection is required for projects over $15,000.

On a Standard 203(k), yes. An FHA-approved 203(k) Consultant is required. On a Limited 203(k), a consultant is optional, although your lender may require one. Separately, a Limited 203(k) over $15,000 requires an inspection, and at $15,000 or less the lender decides whether one is necessary. Genstone works with consultants and lenders on both versions and writes bids that are easy for them to review.

faqs.q: Can I do some of the renovation work myself?
faqs.a: Most lenders do not allow buyers to perform the renovations themselves. The work is completed by a contractor whose bid the lender has reviewed. That protects the buyer and the lender, keeps the work in line with the approved scope, and makes draw inspections straightforward. If you have a specific situation in mind, ask your FHA-approved lender how they handle it before you plan around it.

faqs.q: What kinds of work are not eligible?
faqs.a: Most repairs and renovations are permitted, including pool repairs. Luxury additions such as new pools, spas and outdoor kitchens are not eligible. Your lender has the final word on eligibility for any specific item. During scoping, we flag anything that is likely to raise questions so it can be removed or discussed with the lender before the bid is submitted.

faqs.q: Can I use a 203(k) loan to buy a duplex or fourplex?
faqs.a: Yes. FHA 203(k) loans may be used for eligible two- to four-unit properties, provided the buyer occupies one of the units. That lets an owner-occupant renovate the whole building, live in one unit and rent the others. These projects often involve shared systems such as the roof, heating plant and electrical service, and Genstone plans the scope and phasing with that in mind.

faqs.q: Can renovations happen after I move in?
faqs.a: Depending on the project, renovations may be completed before or after the buyer moves in. Major structural work, extensive system replacement or a whole-house remodel usually makes living in the home difficult, while smaller projects may be manageable with the buyer in place. Your lender sets the rules for occupancy during the work, and we sequence the scope to fit.

faqs.q: What should I do first if I want a 203(k) loan?
faqs.a: Talk with an FHA-approved lender to determine your eligibility and learn how that lender handles 203(k) loans. Once you are working with a lender and have a property in mind, contact Genstone Construction at (312) 429-2637. We will walk the property, discuss the scope and prepare the detailed bid the lender needs to move the loan forward, usually with an early read on which version of the program fits.

faqs.q: I am a lender. What does Genstone provide on a 203(k) file?
faqs.a: An itemized scope and bid that reconciles with the consultant's write-up, a designated field manager, coordinated permits and inspections, verified contractor insurance and licensing, collected lien waivers, and progress documentation with photos and milestones that match each draw request. Changes from unforeseen conditions are documented and reviewed before additional work proceeds. We are an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor and work with institutional clients regularly.
